scenario: AITA for taking my coworker down a notch ? | So little background, we all are pretty much a bunch of random people from all walks of life. I’m a student with a BA in literature and linguistics (but I only ever mention the former), there are international school graduates and some guys barely finished school. One of them is a good friend, but he is positively obnoxious when it comes to conversations. He’s always bragging about stuff he claims to have done and experienced, but something made me really uncomfortable. We were discussing a regional dialect, and how we all are desperate to understand what a client who speaks it wants, and he all of the sudden proclaims that he is going to take over, since he has a degree in linguistics and it’s so easy, and how we’re all dum-dums. I started laughing and asked him why he’d think we believe him. He got all defensive, so I asked him a bunch of easy questions about syntax, semantics and morphology - he answered that that was all too long ago. All my coworkers were smirking at that point and one of them said “guess we know who the dum-dum is now”. My bragging coworker is now really mad at me and has been distant all day. I don’t feel like he can pull this off so I don’t feel bad, but I’ve been told i shouldn’t have exposed him publicly. So, AITA?

If you’re in a field where this matters (e.g., corporate, legal, finance), the attire can reinforce your readiness for challenges and expectations. 2. **Body Language & Posture**: The way you dress subtly influences how you carry yourself. A suit can encourage better posture (shoulders back, chin up), which often correlates with confidence. Even if you’re not aware of it, your body language might be more assertive when dressed this way. 3. **Psychological Priming**: Studies (like those on "enclothed cognition") suggest that certain clothes can subtly affect your mindset. Wearing a suit might make you feel more "in control" or "serious," which can boost your confidence in high-stakes situations. 4. **Social Perception**: People often judge competence based on appearance. If you feel confident *and* others perceive you as authoritative, it can create a positive feedback loop—reinforcing your self-assurance. 5. **Personal Identity**: Confidence isn’t just about outward appearance; it’s also about aligning with how you want to be seen. If a suit feels like "you," it’s a tool for self-expression, not just a uniform. **Potential Considerations**: - **Context Matters**: A suit might feel stifling in creative or casual environments. Balance it with outfits that reflect your personality too. - **Comfort**: If it’s too tight or uncomfortable, confidence can dip. Find a fit that’s polished but *yours*. - **Authenticity**: Confidence comes from within, but clothes can amplify it. If you’re not naturally drawn to formalwear, explore other styles that make you feel powerful (e.g., sharp blazers, tailored coats). **Try This**: Next time you wear a suit, notice how it affects your interactions. Do you speak more clearly? Do others respond differently? Experiment with small tweaks (e.g., a bold tie, a pocket square) to see what enhances your vibe. Ultimately, if it works for you, lean into it! Confidence is a skill—dressing in a way that supports it is just one part of the equation. What’s your favorite part about wearing a suit? The fit?
